short.q: Sound travels at 340 m/s. A person hears an echo 0.50 s after clapping. Calculate the distance to the wall.
short.model: Distance there and back = 340 × 0.50 = 170 m, so the wall is 85 m away.

short.q: Describe how to measure the speed of sound in air using two observers.
short.model: One observer fires a starting pistol; the other, at least 100 m away, times from the flash to hearing the bang. Speed = distance ÷ time. Repeat and average.
points: time from flash to bang with stopwatch

short.q: State two differences between a transverse and a longitudinal wave, giving an example of each.
short.model: Transverse: vibrations perpendicular to travel, has crests and troughs (e.g. light). Longitudinal: vibrations parallel to travel, has compressions and rarefactions (e.g. sound).
points: direction of vibration compared with travel

short.q: Explain why you can hear someone around a corner but not see them.
short.model: Sound has a wavelength similar to the width of the doorway so it diffracts a lot; light has a much smaller wavelength so it hardly diffracts.
points: light wavelength much smaller, little diffraction

short.q: A student sees two traces on an oscilloscope. Trace B is taller with more waves on screen than trace A. Compare the sounds.
short.model: B is louder because its amplitude is larger, and has a higher pitch because its frequency is higher.
points: more waves means higher frequency, higher pitch
